          MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF VISTRA CORP. TO
                      NOVEC’S MOTION FOR CLARIFICATION

            Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (“Commission” or “FERC”),1 Vistra Corp. (“Vistra”) hereby moves to

answer and answers the pleading that Northern Virginia Electric Cooperative, Inc. (“NOVEC”)

filed on July 29, 2026,2 in the above-captioned proceeding. Although styled as a motion for

clarification, NOVEC’s motion is in reality an impermissible, out-of-time request for rehearing

because it contests determinations the Commission made in its June 18, 2026 order in the above-

captioned dockets (“June 2026 Order”).3 Because NOVEC’s pleading was filed after the statutory

deadline for requests for rehearing, it must be denied as untimely.




      1
          18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212, 385.213.
      2
      PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Motion for Clarification of NOVEC, Docket No. EL25-49-000 (filed July 29,
2026) (“NOVEC Filing”).
      3
          PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 195 FERC ¶ 61,209 (2026) (“June 2026 Order”).
  I.       MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER

               Although the Commission’s procedural rules generally do not allow answers to requests

      for rehearing, the Commission may permit them for good cause.4 The Commission frequently

      accepts answers that clarify the issues before the Commission, ensure a complete record, or

      otherwise assist the Commission in its decision-making.5 Vistra respectfully requests that the

      Commission accept this answer to clarify that NOVEC’s motion is in fact, a request for rehearing.

II.       ANSWER

               A. The Commission should reject NOVEC’s motion as an untimely request for
                  rehearing.

               Although NOVEC styles its filing as a motion for clarification, the substance of the filing

      directly contests the merits of the Commission’s June 2026 Order, which renders the pleading a

      request for rehearing. The Commission categorizes pleadings based on their “substance,” not

      “party-bestowed title.”6 As NOVEC acknowledges, the Commission “concluded” in the June

      2026 Order that the record “[did] not adequately substantiate the need for an additional [Grid

      Reliance Charge] at this time” or provide sufficient information on “how such a charge should be




          4
            18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(2) (“An answer may not be made to a protest, an answer, a motion for oral argument, or
      a request for rehearing, unless otherwise ordered by the decisional authority.”).
          5
            See, e.g., PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 182 FERC ¶ 61,073, at P 13 (2023) (accepting answers to answers that
      “provided information that assisted us in our decision-making process.”); New Fortress Energy LLC,
      174 FERC ¶ 61,207, at P 7 (2021) (accepting answers because they provided information that assisted the
      Commission’s decision-making process); Alaska Gasline Dev. Corp., 171 FERC ¶ 61,134, at P 7 (2020) (accepting
      answers that “clarify the concerns raised and provide information that has assisted in our decision making.”); Saltville
      Gas Storage Co., L.L.C., 164 FERC ¶ 61,212, at P 2 n.6 (2018) (accepting answers that “assist the Commission in
      understanding the issues raised, and will ensure a complete record.”).
          6
             San Diego Gas & Elec. Co. v. Sellers of Energy & Ancillary Servs., 133 FERC ¶ 61,014, at P 15 (2010) (“While
      PG&E has styled this filing as a motion for clarification, we are not obligated to accept a filing solely on the basis of
      its party-bestowed title. Instead, we examine the substance of the pleading. We find that PG&E’s motion cannot be
      interpreted to be a motion for clarification because PG&E is not asking that we clarify any previous Commission
      order. Rather, we find PG&E’s motion to be an untimely attempt by PG&E to seek rehearing of a prior Commission
      order.”)

 calculated and assessed.”7 The Commission was crystal clear that “experience with the actual use

of these new transmission services” is necessary to create the record the Commission would need

to support any revised proposal for a Grid Reliance Charge.8 In response, NOVEC “respectfully

disagrees that the record does not substantiate the need for an additional charge.”9                               That

“disagree[ment]” directly contradicts the Commission’s determination on both the now-rejected

Grid Reliance Charge and the evidence on which that determination was based. NOVEC asks the

Commission to “clarify” that it did not mean what it said in determining that “experience with the

actual use” of the new transmission services is a necessary prerequisite for any future proposals

similar to the Grid Reliance Charge.10 Disagreement with clear findings is not grounds for

clarification.11 Rather, it is grounds for requesting rehearing, which NOVEC chose not to pursue

within the timeframe allotted by the Federal Power Act.

           Further, NOVEC mischaracterizes clear Commission statements as ambiguous.                                For

example, NOVEC argues, “it is not clear what additional support the Commission believes it

would have needed to support approval of a rate akin to or serving the purpose of the proposed

Grid Reliance Charge.”12 On the contrary, the Commission was quite explicit:

       Supra note 6 (explaining that a motion for clarification must be asking the Commission to clarify a previous
order); see also Erie Blvd. Hydropower, L.P., 118 FERC ¶ 61,196, at P 11 (2007) (“To the extent that GIPA and
Adirondack seek clarification or reconsideration, styling an improper request for rehearing as a motion for clarification
or motion for reconsideration cannot cure its deficiencies.”).

         NOVEC Filing at 5.

            In particular, the record contains insufficient description of the potential nature or
           magnitude of the cited benefits or the potential costs that transmission providers or
           owners may incur when providing these benefits to Eligible Customers on behalf of Co-
           Located Loads. For example, Indicated TOs state that, even where an Eligible Customer
           has requested FCD or NFCD transmission service for 0 MW, a large Co-Location
           Arrangement will still depend on the transmission system for a suite of synchronization
           support services, such as stable frequency, inertia, stability services (damping, angle
           stability), fault current capability, and ride-through and protection coordination.
           However, beyond briefly listing such benefits, the record lacks specificity regarding
           what these services are, what costs they involve, and how they benefit Eligible
           Customers on behalf of Co-Located Loads.13

          NOVEC disregards this direct statement of missing evidence as merely a request for “cost

support for the rate itself,” ignoring that the Commission also found a lack of specificity on the

nature of the services and their benefits.14

          NOVEC’s explains that it “did not seek rehearing on this issue because NOVEC expects

that the PJM stakeholder process will result in submission of another proposal for the

Commission’s consideration.”15        Setting aside the troubling implication that some PJM

stakeholders might intend to ignore the Commission’s determination on this issue, NOVEC’s

explanation cannot rehabilitate its flawed pleading. Ongoing PJM stakeholder processes have no

bearing on the statutory deadline for seeking rehearing or other Commission rules of procedure.

          Instead of filing a timely request for rehearing, NOVEC filed a mislabeled motion for

clarification 41 days after the June 2026 Order, well outside the statutory requirements for requests

for rehearing. Under Section 313 of the Federal Power Act, requests for rehearing must be made




   13
        June 2026 Order at P 455.
   14

   15

 within 30 days,16 and courts interpret this as a bright-line rule that even the Commission lacks

discretion to extend.17 The Commission must deny NOVEC’s filing as untimely.18

           B. The Commission’s clear conclusion on the Grid Reliance Charge is correct.

           Looking past NOVEC’s procedural error, NOVEC is also wrong on the merits. The

Commission’s rejection of the Grid Reliance Charge was the right decision. The proposed Grid

Reliance Charge would have applied equally to customers who use the grid in completely different

ways, from customers that never reserve service to customers that frequently reserve significant

amounts of service. Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service customers who never

reserve transmission service to pull energy from the grid and rely on it only for black start and

regulation services would have been forced to pay for something other than those services. That

is not consistent with cost causation principles, and it would have been a departure from the

Commission’s long-standing policy requiring transmission providers to offer and price ancillary

services separately.19

           In any event, the Commission’s decision to wait until the new transmission services are

implemented before considering proposals similar to the Grid Reliance Charge makes sense. By

waiting for evidence of how parties use the new transmission services, the Commission can best

evaluate whether gaps remain in the new transmission service rate structure. Vistra’s position is

    that a customer using the grid solely for regulation and black start service is relying very little on

   the grid.20 If substantial evidence gathered through actual use of the new transmission services

   eventually shows otherwise, and PJM is able to demonstrate that the new transmission service rates

   allow certain customers to receive grid services that they do not pay for, the Commission can

   revisit the issue based on that evidence, consistent with the June 2026 Order. Unless and until

   real-world experience with the new transmission services produces such evidence, there is no

   evidence demonstrating that the alleged problem the Grid Reliance Charge was intended to solve

   is even a problem at all—much less that it warrants creation of a new charge for an ill-defined

   service with no identified benefits. Accordingly, the Commission should reject NOVEC’s attempt

   to resurrect this issue in this proceeding and should review skeptically any attempt, by NOVEC or

   others, to relitigate this issue through PJM’s eventual compliance filing in response to the June

   2026 Order.

III.   Conclusion

              NOVEC’s motion is in reality an untimely rehearing request that must be rejected as a

   matter of law. Rejecting NOVEC’s pleading is also consistent with the June 2026 Order. Co-

   location arrangements are poised to relieve the growing stress of large load growth on the PJM

   grid, and this docket aims to create clear and readily implementable rules to facilitate those

   arrangements. Vistra urges the Commission to resist NOVEC’s attempt to inject ambiguity into

   unambiguous Commission holdings.
